🚀 We are NOVA VAMPIRES!

A passionate team of developers and innovators from Ben Guerir, Morocco, competing in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Our mission is to build an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring system to support safer space exploration.

We're looking for creative, motivated teammates with skills in Python, AI, Data Science, Web Development, UI/UX, and Space Science.

Let's innovate, collaborate, and build something extraordinary together! 🌌

details:
WHAT ASTROCARE IS

AstroCare is a health monitoring platform that makes an astronaut's health data understandable and trustworthy. It brings heart response, perceived effort, cognitive check-ins and radiation context into one clear view, and it shows where every number came from.

THE PROBLEM

Astronaut health data comes from many places: sensors, how hard a workout felt, reaction tests and radiation instruments. These arrive in different formats, so they are hard to compare and easy to misread. A simulated value can look exactly like a measured one. On missions to the Moon and Mars, help from Earth is slow, with delays of 3 to 14 seconds expected on lunar missions and up to 22 minutes to Mars.

HOW IT WORKS

Data is collected in three ways:

1. Astronaut input: profile (height, weight, age, mission day), daily check-ins (sleep, fatigue, mood), daily questions, a Borg effort rating (6 to 20), and reaction and attention tasks.

2. Apple Watch inside the habitat: heart rate, HRV, activity and sleep.

3. Suit chips outside: we propose adding three chips to a Liquid Cooling and Ventilation Garment. An ECG patch on the chest gives heart rate and beat-to-beat intervals. A breathing belt on the rib cage gives breathing rate and skin temperature. A fingertip clip gives blood oxygen (SpO2) and pulse.

Three roles use the data:

- Astronaut: sees their own data and acknowledges alerts.

- Habitat screen: shows a crew summary.

- Earth ground station: sees full detail, manages astronaut accounts, and sends alerts and decisions, for example "hold the outing" or "swap the crew member".

DESIGN RULES

- Every number carries a source label: simulation, wearable, self-report or historical.

- Missing readings stay missing. Nothing is filled in or smoothed.

- A lost connection shows a visible stale-data warning.

- A sensor reading flagged poor quality can never trigger an alert.

- The system gives observations with evidence, never diagnoses. A human at the Earth station makes the decisions.

- Warnings must also work locally, without waiting for Earth.

WHAT WE BUILT

- A working astronaut dashboard with 7 pages: overview, heart, cognition, exercise, environment, history and garment. It runs on a seeded simulator, so the same seed always gives the same data.

- Real NASA radiation data: unmodified values from the NASA OSDR RadLab API (ISS, Lidal instrument, 2022-04-01, 288 readings), cached so the demo works offline.

- Explainable observations, such as "Reported effort was higher than in your previous comparable session", each shown with its evidence and the basis of the rule.

- A sources register that ties each data field and rule to an article or dataset (40 sources). Our own default thresholds are labelled as prototype defaults, because no NASA or CSA source we found gives clinical thresholds.

- A concept design for the suit chips, and an analysis of a sample sensor data file, including how to handle a poor-quality oxygen reading.

- The backend API, the Earth ground station and the suit-chip ingestion are designed and specified, and are our next build steps.

WHY IT MATTERS

Longer missions mean longer isolation and slower help from Earth. AstroCare helps crews and mission control see what changed, understand why, and trust where each number came from.

LIMITS

AstroCare is a prototype. It has no life-support function and makes no diagnoses. The simulator and the sensor sample data are synthetic.

NASA DATA AND RESOURCES USED

NASA OSDR RadLab API (radiation data); NASA Human Research Program hazard and risk pages; NASA technical reports on communication delay and on wearable biosensor monitoring; Canadian Space Agency pages on radiation monitoring.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and Playwright for testing. Planned backend: Node.js, Express, SQLite and WebSockets.
